source: JZ Mock E · Paper 2 · Question 16 · Publisher worked answer
label: JZ Mock E · Paper 2 · Question 16
knowledgePattern: Test strict trapezium-error claims and a reflected integral
solution:
For statement 1, f′′>0 makes the polynomial graph strictly upward-bending on the interval. Every chord over a nonzero strip lies strictly above the interior curve. Each trapezium therefore has larger area than the corresponding exact strip, giving Jn>I for every positive integer n. Statement 1 is true.

Statement 2 permits f′′=0. The allowed polynomial f(x)=1+x is positive for x≥0, has positive first derivative and zero second derivative. Every trapezium estimate is exact, so Jn+1=Jn, not strictly smaller. Statement 2 is false.

Reflecting the original graph in x = 2 shows that ∫04f(4−x)dx=I. But increasing the number of strips need not preserve the sign of an error when no curvature condition is imposed. For a concrete example, take f(x)=2+2x−[x(4−x)]3/64. On 0≤x≤4, the subtracted term lies between 0 and 1, so f(x)≥1+2x>0. For x≥4, that term is nonpositive, so f(x)≥2+2x>0. Thus it meets the required positivity on the entire domain.

The endpoint and midpoint heights are f(0)=2, f(2)=5 and f(4)=10. Hence J1=4(2+10)/2=24 and J2=2(2+2×5+10)/2=22.

Expanding, [x(4−x)]3=64x3−48x4+12x5−x6. Its integral from 0 to 4 is 4096/35, so I=24−64/35=776/35. This is less than 24 but greater than 22. Taking n = 1 therefore satisfies the premise of statement 3 and fails its conclusion. Only statement 1 is true: answer A.

hints.title: Compare chords with the curve
hints.body: Sketch a curve bending upwards. A trapezium uses the chord between two sampled points as its top edge. Compare that chord with the curve between the points.
hints.recap: An increasing gradient makes the graph bend upwards.
hints.pitfall: The sign of the height does not determine the approximation error.
hints.pause: Use the chord position to test statement 1.

recall.reminder: An increasing gradient makes the graph bend upwards.

hints.title: Include zero curvature
hints.body: Statement 2 allows the second derivative to equal zero. Try a positive, increasing straight-line function and calculate what the trapezium rule does to it.
hints.recap: A non-strict assumption includes its equality case.
hints.pitfall: Keep the function positive for every nonnegative input.
hints.pause: Check whether the claimed strict decrease still holds.

recall.reminder: Determine the approximation error by comparing each chord with the curve.

hints.title: Compare one trapezium with two
hints.body: Reflect the graph in x=2. Then write the one-strip and two-strip trapezium formulae on the interval 0 to 4.
hints.recap: Reflection across the middle of an interval preserves its integral.
hints.pitfall: Changing the number of strips also changes which heights are sampled.
hints.pause: Which estimate uses the midpoint height? Sketch what happens when that height is lower.

recall.reminder: A horizontal reflection preserves the area of the corresponding region.

hints.title: Test a curve with a lower middle
hints.body: Try f(x)=2+2x−[x(4−x)]364. The subtracted term leaves the endpoint heights unchanged.
hints.recap: To disprove a claim, the example must meet its assumptions and fail its conclusion.
hints.pitfall: Check positivity for every x≥0, including x beyond the integration interval.
hints.pause: Check the assumptions, then compare the two trapezium estimates with the exact integral.

recall.reminder: Reflecting a graph does not change its integral over the matching interval.
